reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Age-related degeneration of the cervical discs and facet joints causing neck pain, stiffness, and sometimes referred occipital headache; it is extremely common and often asymptomatic on imaging
Nerve-root compression by osteophytes or disc material produces radiculopathy with dermatomal arm pain, sensory change, weakness, and reflex loss, most often at C5/6 and C6/7
Cord compression from a narrowed canal produces cervical spondylotic myelopathy, the most important complication, which can develop insidiously
Myelopathy is suggested by gait disturbance, clumsy hands, loss of dexterity, and upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Hoffmann's sign, extensor plantars, sometimes bladder involvement)
Most patients with axial neck pain or radiculopathy improve with conservative measures such as analgesia, activity modification, and physiotherapy
MRI is the investigation of choice to demonstrate cord and root compression when myelopathy or persistent radiculopathy is suspected
Progressive myelopathy is an indication for surgical decompression to halt deterioration, since established cord damage recovers poorly
Radiographic degenerative change correlates poorly with symptoms, so imaging findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture
reference.pathophysiology: With ageing the cervical intervertebral discs lose height and hydration, transferring load to the facet and uncovertebral joints, which develop osteophytes. These bony spurs, together with disc bulging, ligamentum flavum thickening, and reduced canal diameter, encroach on the neural foramina and spinal canal. Foraminal narrowing compresses nerve roots to cause radiculopathy, while central canal stenosis compresses the spinal cord, producing myelopathy through direct pressure and impaired vascular supply. Dynamic factors during neck movement can aggravate cord compression. The degenerative process is gradual, and neurological compromise may accumulate slowly before becoming clinically apparent.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral nerve entrapment (e.g. carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome)
Brachial plexopathy or thoracic outlet syndrome
Motor neuron disease and other neurodegenerative conditions
Multiple sclerosis or intramedullary cord lesion
Shoulder pathology (rotator cuff disease) referring pain to the arm
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the cervical spine to assess cord and root compression
Plain cervical radiographs (including flexion/extension views) for alignment and degenerative change
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to distinguish radiculopathy from peripheral entrapment
CT for detailed bony anatomy when MRI is contraindicated or surgery is planned
Neurological examination for upper and lower limb signs of myelopathy
redFlags: Signs of cervical myelopathy (gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, sphincter dysfunction) requiring urgent specialist assessment
Features suggesting infection or malignancy (fever, weight loss, night pain, cancer history)
Acute deterioration after neck trauma in a spondylotic, stenotic spine
reference.prognosis: Axial neck pain and radiculopathy usually follow a fluctuating but generally benign course with conservative care; cervical spondylotic myelopathy tends to progress in a stepwise manner, and while surgery can arrest decline, neurological recovery of established deficits is often incomplete, making timely intervention important.
pitfalls: Missing early myelopathy by attributing gait or hand-function changes to age or arthritis
Over-relying on degenerative radiographic findings that are common and often asymptomatic
Delaying decompression in progressive myelopathy until irreversible cord damage occurs
Aggressive manipulation of a stenotic, myelopathic cervical spine
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Treat axial neck pain with simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, reserving neuropathic agents for radicular symptoms
Promote activity modification, postural advice and a physiotherapy programme of neck mobilising, strengthening and range-of-motion exercises
Consider a fluoroscopically-guided nerve-root or facet-joint corticosteroid injection for persistent radicular pain
Screen at each review for cervical spondylotic myelopathy by examining for gait disturbance, hand clumsiness and upper motor neurone signs
Refer for spinal surgical assessment when radiculopathy is refractory or when myelopathy is suspected
Arrange decompressive surgery for progressive myelopathy or disabling radiculopathy that is unresponsive to conservative care
